one_sentence: The divine-human relationship described in Scripture exhibits the same relational topology as attachment theory's 2D anxiety-avoidance model, with worship postures mapping onto the same four quadrants as attachment styles.
executive_summary: This document establishes a structural isomorphism between attachment theory in developmental psychology and the theology of prayer and worship. It argues that the 2D anxiety-avoidance model (Bartholomew & Horowitz, 1991) maps precisely onto four worship postures: secure trust, anxious legalism, avoidant deism, and disorganized trauma-theology. Ten independent structural correspondences are identified, including secure base (God as refuge), proximity seeking (prayer), separation protest (lament), internal working models (theology proper), earned security (sanctification), and attachment hierarchy (first commandment). The isomorphism is empirically supported by the Attachment to God Inventory (Beck & McDonald, 2004), which measures anxiety and avoidance in the God-relationship on the same 2D space. The document concludes that this structural correspondence is not an imposed analogy but a discovery of a real relational topology, with bidirectional implications: attachment theory constrains viable pastoral models, and Scripture predicts attachment dynamics discovered millennia later.
short_summary: This document is a structural isomorphism record mapping attachment theory onto Christian theology of prayer and worship. The core claim is that the 2D anxiety-avoidance model of attachment styles (secure, anxious, avoidant, disorganized) maps identically onto four worship postures (secure trust, anxious legalism, avoidant deism, disorganized trauma-theology). Key evidence includes ten independent structural correspondences (secure base, proximity seeking, separation protest, internal working models, earned security, attachment hierarchy) and empirical support from the Attachment to God Inventory. This matters because it provides a testable, empirically grounded framework for understanding the divine-human relationship, with practical implications for pastoral care, spiritual formation, and the integration of psychology and theology.
